Hi Samir / Lena,

Thanks again for a productive partner review last week. As we approach the renewal window for ACME (term ends 2027-12-15), I wanted to capture a concrete amendment proposal for the Reserved GPU pool and overflow policy so your procurement and SRE teams can evaluate.

Quick summary of what we heard from you:
- Peak inference traffic has a 6-hour evening surge (p95 concurrency spikes) that exceeds the current reserved pool by ~30%
- You want predictable throughput and a way to avoid throttling during launches, but procurement prefers not to pay for permanently idle capacity
- Compliance requires clear billing & auditability for any on-demand spillover usage

Proposal attached: "proposed_capacity_addendum_v1.pdf"
High-level options we can include in the renewal amendment (details in the attachment):
1) Reserved top-up: +8 reserved A100-equivalent GPUs (12-month term), guaranteed baseline throughput of 1.5M tokens/min across the pool; lower per-GPU rate for reserved capacity.
2) Adaptive overflow: instead of a hard cap, configure a soft overflow window where on-demand instances can spill 0-40% above reserved capacity at a premium rate. Overflow is metered per-token and appears as a separate line on invoice with timestamped audit logs.
3) Hard cap alternative: if ACME requires a strict ceiling, we can set an enforced hard cap; any requests beyond the cap receive a 429 and an optional queuing layer (best-effort).

Questions for your team to prioritize:
- Preferred overflow mode (adaptive spillover with burst credits vs hard cap)?
- Target worst-case percent over-reserve you want to allow (0/10/20/40)?
- Any SLOs (p95 latency, token/sec) you must guarantee to your customers?

If useful, I can schedule a 30-min SRE + procurement sync with our engineering lead (Dev) to walk the exact metrics and billing examples from the attached model.

Thanks,

Samir —

Great questions. I attached a simple invoice simulation workbook (acme_capacity_model.xlsx) — summary below. If you want, we can convert this into a formal amendment doc for signature once we lock the percent spillover and term length.

Invoice examples (monthly):
- Reserved-only (baseline): 24 reserved A100-equiv GPUs (current commit) + no overflow = $XXX,XXX/month
- Reserved + adaptive overflow: Reserve increases to 32 GPUs (+8 top-up) at a reduced per-GPU reserved rate. Overflow up to 30% above reserve (measured per-hour window) billed at a burst rate (x2 reserved unit rate) and appears as a separate usage line. Example month with 6 peak days with 2-hour surges shows ~8% incremental spend vs reserved-only month in our model.

Auditability: overflow usage is logged as token-level slices with job ids and timestamps; we provide a CSV export each month and streaming logs on request. That meets SOC evidence patterns we’ve supplied to other customers.

SLA/latency: for traffic routed to the reserved pool (no overflow) we can guarantee p95 <= 400ms for the model family you’re running — we’ll include this in the amendment. During adaptive overflow (on-demand instances launched), p95 typically increases to 600–800ms for the first 10–15 minutes of scale-up while KV caches warm; after warm-up we expect parity within ~20% of reserved latency. If you require hard <400ms during all bursts, the hard cap or larger reserved footprint is the safer option.

Next steps I propose:
- Confirm preferred overflow ceiling (0/10/20/30%); we recommended 30% as a balance for ACME given historical spikes.
- Confirm term for the top-up (12 vs 24 months) — 24-month gives deeper discounts.
- SRE sync: Dev can walk the warm-up and cache behaviors.

Looping in Dev for technical follow-up.

Hi Samir / Lena —

Thanks for the signal on requirements. A few technical points to help ACME decide on the right overflow cap and reserve sizing:

1) Warm-up and KV cache: on-demand replicas do a cold KV cache start; practical warm-up to stable p95 is 8–12 minutes depending on sequence lengths and model. We can accelerate warm-up by pre-loading prefixes (we offer a warm-up API) at a small extra cost.
2) Continuous batching: our runtime will batch across incoming requests; during bursts this improves throughput efficiency which reduces effective per-token cost compared to naive scaling.
3) Priority routing: we can mark reserved pool traffic as high-priority; overflow gets routed to on-demand capacity with lower priority and optional throttling rules. This preserves SLA for reserved traffic even during heavy burst conditions.
4) Suggested reserve buffer: given ACME’s 30% spike profile, we recommend a 20% reserved-top-up (vs current) plus adaptive overflow capped at 15% to balance cost and latency — this reduces warm-up incidence while keeping incremental cost moderate.

If you want, I can run a simulated replay of last quarter’s traffic against the different configs and produce a 1-pager that shows expected spike hit rates, warm-up frequency, and incremental cost.

Happy to jump on a technical call with your SRE next week (suggest Tue or Wed morning PST).

Cheers,
